projects.name: Cider making
projects.status: The 16-gallon batch is finished and its seal is open, so racking it into the corny kegs comes first. Three 7-gallon fermenters of fresh juice were pitched on Nov 15.

next.text: Buy food-grade tubing at the brew shop
Clean the corny kegs with PBW, rinse, and replace all the O-rings
Sanitize the kegs with Star San
Rack the 16-gallon batch straight into the kegs
Purge the headspace with CO2 and pressurize the kegs for long-term aging
Add yeast nutrient to the three 7-gallon fermenters as soon as fermentation starts
Add the second nutrient dose about a third of the way through fermentation

think.text: This yeast tends to throw sulfur at certain temperatures and when nitrogen is short, which is why the nutrient timing matters.
The open batch is taking on oxygen. If the tubing run slips, a blanket of CO2 from your tank over the surface buys some time.
16 gallons fills three 5-gallon kegs with about a gallon left over. Have a fourth keg or a smaller vessel ready.
A third of the way through is a third of the sugar gone. If the new juice started near 14 Brix like the last batch, that is around 1.038 on the hydrometer.
A rotten-egg smell early on is the cue to add nutrient and hold the temperature steady. It is easier to prevent than to remove.

refs.title: Racking into kegs, in order
body: Release any pressure, then take each keg apart: lid, posts and dip tubes.
Soak or scrub everything in hot PBW, then rinse until the water runs clear.
Fit new O-rings on the lid, posts and dip tubes, and reassemble.
Add Star San, seal, shake to coat every surface, then push it out through the liquid post with CO2. The keg is left sanitized and full of gas.
Run sanitizer through the full length of the new tubing.
Fill each keg with the tube resting on the bottom to limit splashing. Leave the sediment behind.
Seal, pressurize, and pull the relief valve 3 or 4 times to purge the headspace. Spray the lid and posts with sanitizer and watch for bubbles.
Clean the 16-gallon fermenter the same day, before the yeast cake dries on.

refs.title: Nutrient plan for the 7-gallon fermenters
body: Dose 1: as soon as you see active fermentation (bubbling airlock or foam).
Dose 2: about a third of the way through, judged by gravity readings.
Use the dose on the nutrient package for 7 gallons, split across the two additions.
Keep the fermenters somewhere cool and steady. A steady temperature matters more than a perfect one.

projects.name: Cricket breeding
projects.status: Breeding is under way with your son. A few males died off and some crickets were lost to low humidity. The aim for now is simply to see whether you can breed them.

next.text: Raise the humidity in the containers
Build a clear plexiglass or plastic fighting ring with a central divider
Keep the males apart for 3 to 4 days, then see whether they will fight
Later: mount a top-down camera and use computer vision as an unbiased judge

think.text: For humidity, a damp (not wet) laying dish and fresh vegetable slices add moisture without open water. Keep the air holes, since still, wet air grows mold.
A small hygrometer in one tub would tell you whether a change is working.
Keep new store-bought males apart for about a week before mixing them in, in case the batch is sick.

refs.title: Fight trials, from your breeding guide
body: Give each male at least 3 days alone first. Crickets kept in a crowd act like losers; time alone brings their aggression back.
Pair males that are close in weight. Let both settle with the divider in, then lift it.
If they ignore each other, tickle their antennae with a soft brush or grass stem.
Score each fight 0 to 4: 0 ignored each other, 1 antenna fencing, 2 jaws spread, 3 jaws locked, 4 wrestling.
The loser is the one that first avoids contact, runs, or stops chirping. Stop the fight the moment one backs off.
At most one fight per male per day.

refs.title: Key numbers
body: Hold the tubs at 82 to 88°F. Past 95°F is dangerous.
Eggs hatch in about 13 days at 86°F.
Females lay from about 8 to 10 days old as adults.
About 12 weeks per generation.
